title: Transformations
description: Understanding reflection, rotation, translation, and enlargement of 2D shapes on a coordinate grid.

notes.heading: Reflection
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A reflection creates a mirror image of a shape across a mirror line. Every point on the image is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line as the matching point on the original shape.

🔑 Key Concept
Reflecting in the most common lines has simple coordinate rules:
• x-axis: $(x,y) \to (x,-y)$
• y-axis: $(x,y) \to (-x,y)$
• line $y=x$: $(x,y) \to (y,x)$
For a vertical mirror line $x=a$, the $y$-coordinate stays the same and the new $x$-coordinate is $x' = 2a - x$.
For a horizontal mirror line $y=b$, the $x$-coordinate stays the same and the new $y$-coordinate is $y' = 2b - y$.

💡 Worked Example
Reflect point $P(5,3)$ in the line $x=2$.

  Step 1: Find the horizontal distance from $P$ to the mirror line:
    $5 - 2 = 3$ units.

  Step 2: Move the same distance on the other side of $x=2$:
    $2 - 3 = -1$.

So $P' = (-1,3)$.

✅ Check
The midpoint of $PP'$ should lie on the mirror line:
$$\left(\frac{5 + (-1)}{2}, \frac{3 + 3}{2}\right) = (2,3)$$
which is on $x=2$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping both coordinates when reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line. Only the coordinate perpendicular to the mirror line changes; the other coordinate stays exactly the same.

notes.heading: Rotation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point called the centre of rotation. A full description needs three things: the centre, the angle (for example $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $270^\circ$), and the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise).

🔑 Key Concept
When rotating around the origin $(0,0)$:
• $90^\circ$ clockwise: $(x,y) \to (y,-x)$
• $90^\circ$ anticlockwise: $(x,y) \to (-y,x)$
• $180^\circ$: $(x,y) \to (-x,-y)$

A $180^\circ$ rotation has no direction — clockwise and anticlockwise give the same result.

💡 Worked Example
Rotate $A(2,3)$ by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise around $(0,0)$.

  Using the rule $(x,y) \to (-y,x)$:
    $A' = (-3,2)$.

✅ Tip
You can check by imagining turning the page a quarter turn to the left: the point that was to the right and up moves to the left and up a little.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Thinking $90^\circ$ clockwise and $90^\circ$ anticlockwise give the same answer. Remember that $90^\circ$ clockwise is the same as $270^\circ$ anticlockwise, and $90^\circ$ anticlockwise is the same as $270^\circ$ clockwise.

notes.heading: Translation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A translation slides a shape without rotating, reflecting, or resizing it. Every point of the shape moves by the same amount in the same direction.

🔑 Key Concept
A translation is written as a column vector:
$$\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}$$
where $a$ = horizontal movement (positive = right, negative = left) and $b$ = vertical movement (positive = up, negative = down).

To find the image of a point, add the vector to the coordinates:
$$(x,y) \to (x+a,\; y+b)$$

💡 Worked Example
A triangle has vertex $B(-1,4)$. It is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$. Find $B'$.

  New $x$-coordinate: $-1 + 3 = 2$
  New $y$-coordinate: $4 + (-2) = 2$

So $B' = (2,2)$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Translations preserve size, shape, and orientation.
• The vector tells you how far and in what direction; it is not the final coordinate unless you add it to $(0,0)$.
• Two translations can be combined by adding their vectors:
$$\begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ b_1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} a_2 \\ b_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_1+a_2 \\ b_1+b_2 \end{pmatrix}$$

✅ Check
If you translate a shape by a vector and then translate it back by the opposite vector, you return to the starting position. The opposite of $\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}$ is $\begin{pmatrix} -a \\ -b \end{pmatrix}$.

notes.heading: Enlargement
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An enlargement changes the size of a shape by a scale factor, keeping the same shape. It is performed about a centre of enlargement. At Year 7 the centre is usually the origin $(0,0)$.

🔑 Key Concept
If the centre of enlargement is $(0,0)$ and the scale factor is $k$, each coordinate is multiplied by $k$:
$$(x,y) \to (kx,\; ky)$$
• $k > 1$ → the image is bigger and farther from the centre.
• $0 < k < 1$ → the image is smaller and closer to the centre.
• $k = 1$ → the image is identical to the original.

💡 Worked Example
Enlarge triangle $P(1,2)$, $Q(3,2)$, $R(1,5)$ by scale factor $2$ about $(0,0)$.

  Multiply each coordinate by $2$:
    $P' = (2,4)$
    $Q' = (6,4)$
    $R' = (2,10)$

Each side length is doubled, but the angles stay the same.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that a scale factor between $0$ and $1$ is still an enlargement — it just produces a smaller image. Also, the centre of enlargement is not always the origin; if it is a different point, you measure distances from that point rather than multiplying coordinates directly.

✅ Check
Draw lines from the centre through matching vertices. All the lines should be straight and pass through the centre, and each image distance should be $k$ times the original distance from the centre.

notes.heading: Congruent and Similar
notes.body:
📌 Definition
• Congruent shapes are exactly the same shape and size. Corresponding sides and angles are equal.
• Similar shapes are the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

🔑 Key Concept
Transformations that keep a shape congruent are called isometries:
• Reflection, rotation, and translation all produce congruent images.
• Enlargement produces a similar image, not a congruent one (unless the scale factor is $1$).

💡 Worked Example
A rectangle has sides $2$ cm and $4$ cm. It is enlarged by scale factor $3$ about a centre. Is the image congruent or similar to the original?

  New sides: $2 \times 3 = 6$ cm and $4 \times 3 = 12$ cm.
  The shape is still a rectangle with the same angles, but the sides are three times as long.
  Therefore the image is similar, not congruent.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Congruent: same shape, same size.
• Similar: same shape, different size (or same size if scale factor $=1$).
• Angles are always preserved in reflections, rotations, translations, and enlargements.

✅ Check
Count the length of each side and compare. If every matching pair is equal, the shapes are congruent. If every matching pair is in the same ratio, the shapes are similar.

notes.heading: Combined Transformations
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A combined transformation happens when you apply one transformation after another. The final image depends on the order and on each individual transformation.

🔑 Key Concept
Some combinations can be replaced by a single transformation:
• Two reflections in parallel lines = one translation.
• Two reflections in intersecting lines = one rotation.
• A translation followed by another translation is the same as a single translation with the sum of the vectors.

For reflections and rotations, order usually matters. Reflecting in the $x$-axis and then the $y$-axis gives the same result as a $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin, but reflecting in $y=x$ then the $x$-axis is different from the $x$-axis then $y=x$.

💡 Worked Example
Point $A(3,1)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis, then the result is reflected in the $y$-axis. What are the final coordinates?

  Step 1: Reflect in the $x$-axis:
    $(3,1) \to (3,-1)$.

  Step 2: Reflect the new point in the $y$-axis:
    $(3,-1) \to (-3,-1)$.

The combined effect is a $180^\circ$ rotation about $(0,0)$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying the second transformation to the original point instead of to the image from the first step. Always work with the most recent image when combining transformations.

✅ Tip
Write down the coordinates after each step. It is much easier to spot an error if you have a clear list of intermediate points.

notes.heading: Describing Transformations
notes.body:
📌 Definition
To describe a transformation fully, you must give enough information for someone else to draw the image without guessing.

🔑 Key Concept
Required details for each transformation:
• Reflection: state the mirror line (for example $x=2$ or the $y$-axis).
• Rotation: state the centre, the angle, and the direction.
• Translation: state the column vector.
• Enlargement: state the centre and the scale factor.

Saying only "reflection" or "enlargement" is not enough.

💡 Worked Example
A shape moves from position $A$ to position $B$. Each point of $B$ is $4$ units to the right and $1$ unit down from the matching point of $A$. Describe the transformation.

  It is a translation by the vector
  $$\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Use tracing paper to find or check rotations.
• Use a ruler to check perpendicular distances for reflections.
• When describing an enlargement, always mention both the centre and the scale factor.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Describing a rotation without giving the centre. Two shapes can look rotated by $90^\circ$ clockwise, but if the centres differ the images will be in different places. Always state centre, angle, and direction.

✅ Check
A good description should answer: "Could someone else reproduce the image exactly from my words?" If not, add the missing detail.

flashcards.definition: A transformation that produces a mirror image of a shape across a mirror line.
The line across which a shape is reflected.
Turning a shape around a fixed point by a given angle and direction.
The fixed point around which a shape is rotated.
flashcards.example: The origin $(0,0)$ or a vertex of the shape.

flashcards.definition: Sliding a shape so that every point moves the same distance in the same direction.
flashcards.example: A translation by vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ moves every point 3 right and 2 down.

flashcards.definition: A column vector showing horizontal (top) and vertical (bottom) movement.
A transformation that changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a centre.
flashcards.example: Enlarging $(1,3)$ by scale factor $2$ about $(0,0)$ gives $(2,6)$.

flashcards.definition: The multiplier used in an enlargement.
flashcards.example: Scale factor $\frac{1}{2}$ halves every side length.

flashcards.definition: Exactly the same shape and size; corresponding sides and angles are equal.
flashcards.example: A shape and its reflection are congruent.

flashcards.definition: Same shape but a different size; corresponding angles are equal and sides are in proportion.
flashcards.example: An enlargement with scale factor $3$ creates a similar shape.

flashcards.definition: Rotating a point $180^\circ$ about the origin reverses both coordinates.
The sequence in which transformations are applied; changing the order usually changes the result.
flashcards.example: Reflecting in the $x$-axis then the $y$-axis is a $180^\circ$ rotation, but the intermediate image differs from doing the reflections in the reverse order.

questions.stem: Which transformation slides a shape without turning, flipping, or resizing it?
questions.explanation: A translation moves every point of a shape by the same vector, so the shape keeps its size, shape, and orientation.

questions.stem: Point $(4,5)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: Reflecting in the $y$-axis changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate: $(x,y) \to (-x,y)$. So $(4,5) \to (-4,5)$.

questions.stem: Point $(2,1)$ is rotated $90^\circ$ clockwise around $(0,0)$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: The rule for $90^\circ$ clockwise is $(x,y) \to (y,-x)$. Applying it to $(2,1)$ gives $(1,-2)$.

questions.stem: Point $(-3,4)$ is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$. What is the image?
questions.explanation: Add the vector to the point: $-3 + 5 = 2$ and $4 + (-2) = 2$. The image is $(2,2)$.

questions.stem: Point $(2,3)$ is enlarged by scale factor $3$ about $(0,0)$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: For an enlargement about the origin, multiply each coordinate by the scale factor: $(2 \times 3, 3 \times 3) = (6,9)$.

questions.stem: Point $(8,2)$ is enlarged by scale factor $\frac{1}{2}$ about $(0,0)$. What is the image?
questions.explanation: A scale factor between $0$ and $1$ makes the image smaller. Multiply each coordinate by $\frac{1}{2}$: $(8 \times \frac{1}{2}, 2 \times \frac{1}{2}) = (4,1)$.

questions.stem: Which transformation can change the size of a shape?
questions.explanation: Only enlargement changes size. Reflections, translations, and rotations all produce congruent images that are the same size.

questions.stem: Point $(6,2)$ is reflected in the line $x=1$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: The distance from $x=6$ to $x=1$ is $5$ units. Moving $5$ units the other side gives $x = 1 - 5 = -4$. The $y$-coordinate stays $2$, so the image is $(-4,2)$.

questions.stem: Point $(-3,2)$ is rotated $180^\circ$ around $(0,0)$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: A $180^\circ$ rotation reverses both coordinates: $(x,y) \to (-x,-y)$. So $(-3,2) \to (3,-2)$.

questions.stem: A translation by vector $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ is followed by a translation by vector $\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$. What is the single equivalent vector?
questions.explanation: Add the two vectors: $2 + (-3) = -1$ and $-1 + 4 = 3$. The single equivalent vector is $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

questions.stem: A shape is reflected in the $x$-axis and the resulting image is reflected in the $y$-axis. What single transformation is this equivalent to?
questions.explanation: Reflecting $(x,y)$ in the $x$-axis gives $(x,-y)$, and reflecting that in the $y$-axis gives $(-x,-y)$. That is exactly the rule for a $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin.

questions.stem: Which of these transformations always produces a congruent image?
questions.explanation: Reflections, rotations, and translations preserve size and shape, so they always produce congruent images. Enlargements change size, so they produce similar images instead.

questions.stem: A robot starts at $(2,-1)$. It moves by the translation vector $\begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, then reflects the result in the $x$-axis. Where does it finish?
questions.explanation: After the translation: $(2 + (-4), -1 + 3) = (-2,2)$. Reflecting in the $x$-axis changes the sign of the $y$-coordinate: $(-2,2) \to (-2,-2)$.

questions.stem: A rectangular photo is $6$ cm by $4$ cm. It is enlarged by scale factor $2.5$. What are the new dimensions?
questions.explanation: Multiply each dimension by $2.5$: $6 \times 2.5 = 15$ cm and $4 \times 2.5 = 10$ cm. The enlarged photo is $15$ cm by $10$ cm and similar to the original.

questions.stem: Point $P(a,b)$ is reflected in the line $y=x$ and then reflected in the $y$-axis. What are the final coordinates?
questions.explanation: Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the coordinates: $(a,b) \to (b,a)$. Reflecting in the $y$-axis changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate: $(b,a) \to (-b,a)$.
